strengths: Addresses a well-defined and difficult geometric vision problem: practical relative pose estimation for three calibrated views from four correspondences. The proposed mean-point and affine approximations are simple, easy to implement, and reuse mature 5-point and P3P solvers.

The manuscript gives credible technical motivation, including the geometric argument for why the mean-point correspondence has bounded epipolar error and why it adds a nontrivial perspective-camera constraint.

The experimental evidence is broad: synthetic studies, real evaluations on PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen, two RANSAC frameworks, speed-accuracy curves, threshold sensitivity, outlier experiments, alternative pose metrics, and ablations for delta, refinement, filtering, and ENM.

The work is practically useful. The best variants generally improve over the prior HC solver and the 5pt+P3P baseline in pose accuracy or speed-accuracy tradeoff, and the paper reports public code and data links.
weaknesses: The core contribution is approximate rather than an exact 4p3v solver. The theory only loosely bounds the generated correspondence error and does not provide guarantees on final pose accuracy, convergence, or failure probability.

The strongest results depend heavily on a collection of engineering steps: early non-minimal refitting, LM refinement, filtering, tuned delta shifts, and the surrounding RANSAC/LO implementation. This makes the solver contribution somewhat less clean than the headline suggests.

The gains over a strengthened 5pt+P3P baseline are often modest, especially when the baseline also receives refinement/filtering/ENM; the most accurate M±delta variants can also be slower than simpler baselines in full RANSAC runtime.

Comparison to the older Nister-Schaffalitzky solver is incomplete because the authors could not run its full epipole-sampling implementation, so the historical baseline discussion relies partly on reported results and an oracle-style analysis.

The method remains scene- and configuration-dependent, particularly before ENM, and the affine variant can fail badly without refitting. The paper acknowledges this but does not fully characterize degeneracies or practical failure modes.
Presentation is dense: several key tables are hard to read, and the many solver variants make it somewhat difficult to isolate which component is responsible for the final improvement.

strengths: Addresses a real and difficult calibrated three-view geometry problem, where existing exact or homotopy-based 4p3v approaches are complex, fragile, or hard to use in practical RANSAC pipelines.

The proposed solvers are simple and potentially useful: they reuse mature 4-point affine, 5-point essential matrix, and P3P components, and the mean-point construction gives an implementable way to obtain a practical four-correspondence hypothesis generator.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for this problem, covering PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen Day-Night, multiple RANSAC frameworks, threshold sensitivity, runtime/accuracy curves, ablations for refinement/filtering/ENM/delta, and an alternative three-pair pose metric.

The paper includes a reasonable geometric argument for why the mean-point correspondence can be useful, and the synthetic and real-data analyses support the claim that the approximation is often good enough when embedded in robust estimation and local optimization.
Reproducibility is relatively strong: the manuscript reports implementation details, parameter choices, validation setup, code links, and data links.
weaknesses: The core novelty is moderate rather than deep. The method is a practical heuristic built from existing solvers plus RANSAC/local optimization machinery, not an exact or principled solver for the 4p3v polynomial problem.

The theoretical support is limited. The bound on mean-point epipolar error is quite loose, depends on triangle size, and does not translate into pose accuracy, convergence, or stability guarantees; difficult or degenerate configurations are mostly handled empirically.

The best reported improvements over a strong 5pt+P3P baseline are often small. For example, in PoseLib the strongest M+/-delta+R+F+ENM variant improves AUC@10 only modestly over 5pt+P3P+R+F+ENM while roughly doubling runtime on the aggregate datasets.

Several conclusions rely on the full robust-estimation pipeline, especially ENM and LM refinement, making it hard to isolate the value of the approximate minimal hypothesis itself. The raw affine solver performs very poorly in PoseLib before refitting.

The evaluation is extensive but still concentrated on sparse feature triplets from standard landmark/SfM datasets with SuperPoint+LightGlue; usefulness in full SfM/localization systems, under partial visibility patterns where four-view sampling should matter most, or with other matchers is not fully demonstrated.
The comparison to the older Nister-Schaffalitzky solver is incomplete because that implementation could not be run; the paper instead argues from an oracle/partial-code experiment and prior reports.

The provided manuscript version is not anonymized and contains author names, affiliations, acknowledgments, arXiv information, and code/data links; this is a CVPR submission-compliance issue rather than a scientific flaw, but it is material for the submitted form.

strengths: Addresses an important and difficult calibrated three-view relative pose problem, and the proposed approximate 4p3v solvers are practical: they are built from standard 4-point affine fundamental matrix, 5-point essential matrix, and P3P components rather than fragile large polynomial solvers.
The mean-point correspondence idea is simple, easy to implement, and supported by a useful geometric argument plus synthetic and real-data studies showing when it is a reasonable approximation.

The experimental evaluation is unusually broad for this problem: PoseLib and GC-RANSAC, three real datasets, many scenes, 90k triplets, speed-accuracy curves, threshold sensitivity, outlier studies, alternative error metrics, and ablations for refinement, filtering, ENM, and delta shifts.
Reproducibility is strong: the paper reports code and data availability and gives enough implementation detail to reproduce the RANSAC integration and solver variants.
weaknesses: The core method is approximate and heuristic. The theoretical bound for the mean-point correspondence is weak as a pose-estimation guarantee, since the bound can still be large and does not characterize when the resulting essential matrix or P3P initialization will be accurate.

The strongest results depend heavily on extra RANSAC machinery, especially local refinement, filtering, and early non-minimal refitting. The base 4p3v(A) solver fails badly in PoseLib without ENM, and the base 4p3v(M) solver is often close to or worse than the 5pt+P3P baseline.

The gains over a strengthened 5pt+P3P baseline are modest in several headline tables. For example, the best M-delta variants improve AUC only slightly over 5pt+P3P+R+F+ENM while often being substantially slower, so the practical advantage is not uniformly compelling outside lower-sample/high-outlier settings.

The comparison to the older Nister-Schaffalitzky solver is incomplete because the authors could not run the full method and only discuss an oracle variant. This is understandable but leaves one historical baseline not fully resolved.

The paper is dense and somewhat repetitive, with many solver variants and tables. The main acceptance-relevant story is present, but the presentation makes it harder than necessary to distinguish the essential contribution from engineering combinations of existing solvers.

strengths: Addresses an important and difficult 4-point/3-calibrated-view relative pose setting with practical solvers built from standard 4pt affine-F, 5pt essential, and P3P components, making the approach much simpler than HC or epipole-search alternatives.

The mean-point approximation is a neat engineering idea, and the paper provides useful geometric intuition, a bound on the induced epipolar error, and a discussion of why it gives an independent constraint for perspective cameras.

Experimental support is broad: PoseLib and GC-RANSAC, PhotoTourism/Cambridge/Aachen, roughly 90k triplets, synthetic/noise/outlier/threshold studies, per-scene plots, and ablations for delta, refinement, filtering, and ENM.
The refined M/M±δ variants consistently improve over the HC 4p3v baseline and often improve over 5pt+P3P in pose AUC; code and data links are provided, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core solvers are approximate rather than exact 4p3v solutions, and the theoretical analysis only bounds the mean-point epipolar error loosely; it does not establish when the final pose hypothesis will be close to the correct solution.

The best reported gains over the strongest modified 5pt+P3P baseline are modest. For example, the top PoseLib M±δ+R+F+ENM variant improves AUC@10 by less than about one point on the main datasets while often taking substantially longer.

Much of the final performance comes from ENM, filtering, and LM/local optimization inside RANSAC, which partly blurs the contribution of the minimal 4-point hypothesis generator itself and reduces the expected sample-size/runtime advantage.

The comparison to Nister and Schaffalitzky [37] remains incomplete because the authors could not run the actual epipole-sampling code and only report an oracle-style comparison plus literature claims.

The method is scene- and threshold-sensitive before refitting, with the pure affine variant failing badly in PoseLib, and the paper gives limited guidance for degenerate cases such as near-collinear samples, very small triangles, or extreme camera configurations.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-defined and genuinely difficult calibrated three-view pose problem, and the proposed solvers are practical because they reduce 4p3v estimation to efficient, standard components such as 5-point relative pose, P3P, and affine fundamental matrix solvers.

The mean-point correspondence idea is simple, original enough for this problem setting, and supported by geometric motivation, ablations, and supplementary analysis of why it contributes a perspective epipolar constraint.

The empirical evaluation is broad: PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen Day-Night; PoseLib and GC-RANSAC; speed-accuracy curves, threshold sensitivity, outlier experiments, alternative metrics, and comparisons to 5pt+P3P and the recent HC solver.

Reproducibility is above average for this area: the manuscript provides implementation and data links, specifies feature matching, RANSAC settings, thresholds, validation choices, and solver runtimes.
weaknesses: The central solvers are approximate heuristics rather than exact 4p3v solutions. The theoretical support is relatively weak: the bound on the mean-point epipolar error is loose and can be large for large triangles, so it does not characterize when the approximation will be accurate.

The practical gains over a carefully modified 5pt+P3P baseline are often modest. In PoseLib, the best M±δ variants improve AUC by small margins but are notably slower; several M-based variants are close to, rather than clearly better than, 5pt+P3P+R+F+ENM.

The strongest results depend on a stack of engineering choices: early non-minimal refitting, local optimization, filtering, LM refinement, RANSAC thresholds, and the δ shift. This makes the core solver contribution harder to isolate and suggests that performance may be framework-dependent.

The comparison to Nister and Schaffalitzky [37] remains incomplete: the authors report difficulty running the full method and only discuss an oracle epipole variant, so claims against that prior solver are less conclusive than the HC and 5pt+P3P comparisons.

Some claims are overstated. The paper says the methods achieve state-of-the-art results, but the evidence is better summarized as a favorable speed-accuracy tradeoff in several robust-estimation settings rather than a uniformly dominant solver.

The presentation is generally clear, but the paper has many solver variants and dense tables, making it difficult to identify which variant is actually recommended and what tradeoff a practitioner should expect.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-known difficult calibrated three-view relative pose setting and proposes simple, practical approximate solvers built from established 4-point affine fundamental matrix, 5-point essential matrix, and P3P components. This makes the contribution potentially useful and much easier to implement than prior homotopy-continuation or epipole-sampling approaches.

The mean-point correspondence idea is elegant and reasonably justified: the manuscript gives geometric intuition, a bound on the epipolar-line error, and empirical evidence that the mean point is near-optimal within sampled triangle barycentric coordinates across real scenes.

The evaluation is unusually broad for this type of geometric solver paper: PoseLib and GC-RANSAC experiments on PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen, with ablations for ENM, filtering, refinement, delta shifts, thresholds, noise, outlier ratios, and an alternative three-pair pose metric.

The strongest variants consistently improve pose accuracy over 4p3v(HC) and the 5pt+P3P baseline in the reported real-data RANSAC settings; for example, in PoseLib the best M±delta variant improves AUC@10 over 5pt+P3P+R+F+ENM on PhotoTourism, Cambridge, and Aachen, albeit by modest margins.

Reproducibility appears good from the manuscript: the authors claim public source code and data releases, and the method depends mostly on standard solvers rather than fragile bespoke algebraic machinery.
weaknesses: The main contribution is approximate and heuristic rather than an exact solver for the 4p3v problem. The theoretical support for the mean-point construction is limited: the epipolar-error bound can be loose, depends on triangle size, and does not directly guarantee accurate essential-matrix or three-camera pose estimates.

The best-performing results rely heavily on RANSAC engineering additions such as early non-minimal refitting, LM refinement on the fourth point, filtering, and the delta augmentation. Without these, some proposed solvers, especially 4p3v(A), perform poorly in PoseLib, which weakens the claim that the solver itself is robust.

The gains over a carefully strengthened 5pt+P3P baseline are real but often small, while the most accurate M±delta+R+F+ENM variant is substantially slower than simpler baselines in the reported PoseLib tables. This makes the practical advantage more nuanced than the headline state-of-the-art claim suggests.

The evaluation is extensive but concentrated on landmark-style datasets with SuperPoint/LightGlue matches and COLMAP-derived ground truth. There is limited analysis of failure modes for low-parallax, near-planar, repeated-structure, dynamic, or non-landmark imagery, and no downstream SfM/localization pipeline study showing end-task impact.

Comparison to the older Nister-Schaffalitzky epipole-curve approach is incomplete because the authors could not run the full method and only discuss an oracle variant in the supplement. This is understandable but leaves one prior baseline less directly settled.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and genuinely difficult geometry problem: practical relative pose estimation for three calibrated cameras from four point correspondences. The proposed decomposition into approximate two-view geometry followed by P3P is simple, computationally plausible, and useful for RANSAC-style estimation.

The mean-point solver is an elegant contribution. It uses an approximate fifth correspondence derived from the input points, gives some geometric justification for why this can constrain the perspective essential matrix, and remains easy to implement using standard 5-point and P3P solvers.

The experimental evaluation is unusually broad for a minimal-solver paper: 12 PhotoTourism scenes, 5 Cambridge Landmarks scenes, Aachen Day-Night, roughly 90k triplets, two RANSAC frameworks, threshold studies, outlier studies, synthetic studies, ablations for delta, refinement, filtering, ENM, and an alternative pose-error metric.

The reported results support the main practical claim. For example, in PoseLib RANSAC the strongest variant improves AUC@10 over 4p3v(HC) and plain 5pt+P3P on PhotoTourism, Cambridge, and Aachen, and the GC-RANSAC results show a similar ranking.
The work is reproducibility-minded: it states the feature/matching setup, RANSAC settings, datasets, hardware for timing, and provides code and data links.
weaknesses: The proposed solvers are approximate rather than exact solutions to 4p3v. The theoretical support is limited: the mean-point epipolar-error bound is quite loose and does not translate into a clear pose-error guarantee or characterize when the approximation will fail.

A substantial part of the performance comes from practical refinements rather than the core minimal hypothesis itself. The raw affine solver performs very poorly in PoseLib, and even the raw mean-point solver can trail the 5pt+P3P baseline; ENM, local refinement, and filtering are essential to the best results.

The gains over a strengthened 5pt+P3P baseline are meaningful but often modest relative to the added solver complexity and runtime. For instance, the best delta-based ENM variant improves AUC@10 by less than one point over 5pt+P3P+R+F+ENM on several datasets while being notably slower in the early-termination table.

The comparison to Nister and Schaffalitzky [37] is incomplete because the authors could not run the original epipole-sampling code and instead report an oracle-style discussion. This is understandable, but it leaves one historical baseline only partially resolved.

The evaluation is strong but still mostly centered on calibrated central-camera landmark datasets with SuperPoint/LightGlue triplet matches. More evidence in complete SfM/VO/localization pipelines, under calibration errors, very low overlap, or more diverse camera motions would better establish deployment robustness.

Some presentation is dense: key tables are very small, the many solver variants make the story harder to parse, and a few typos/inconsistencies in the supplementary references to modifications slightly reduce clarity.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important and difficult calibrated three-view relative pose setting, the 4p3v configuration, where existing exact or learned homotopy-based methods are not yet broadly practical.

The core idea is appealingly simple: use four triplets to build an approximate two-view geometry, either via an affine model or via an added mean-point correspondence, then register the third view with P3P. This makes the solver easy to implement from standard 5-point, affine fundamental matrix, and P3P components.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for this problem: PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen Day-Night, with 90k image triplets, two RANSAC frameworks, speed-accuracy curves, threshold sensitivity, ablations, synthetic/noise studies, and an alternative pose-error definition.

The paper includes meaningful baselines, especially the 5pt+P3P configuration, and shows that the proposed variants, particularly 4p3v(M±δ)+R(+F/+ENM), usually improve pose AUC over 4p3v(HC) and often over 5pt+P3P in the reported three-view RANSAC setting.
Reproducibility is strong: the manuscript reports implementation choices, selected hyperparameters, runtime conditions, and provides code and dataset links.
weaknesses: The contribution is best understood as a practical approximate hypothesis generator rather than a solver for the exact 4p3v problem. The unmodified solvers can be weak, especially 4p3v(A), and the strong results rely on several heuristic additions: mean-point shifts, early non-minimal refitting, filtering, LM refinement, and RANSAC local optimization.

The performance gains over the strongest 5pt+P3P variants are often modest. In Table 2, the best 4p3v(M±δ)+R+F+ENM accuracy improves AUC@10 by less than about one point on the three main datasets relative to 5pt+P3P+R+F+ENM, while taking substantially more runtime under early termination.

The theoretical support for the mean-point correspondence is suggestive but limited. The provided epipolar-error bound is loose, since the bound can be as large as the triangle itself, and it does not by itself predict when the approximation will be accurate.

The comparison to the older Nister and Schaffalitzky 4p3v method is incomplete because the authors could not run the full epipole-sampling code. This is understandable, but it weakens the breadth of the state-of-the-art claim.

The method has some scene and threshold dependence, acknowledged by the authors. Although ENM reduces this in experiments, the paper does not fully characterize failure modes such as extreme perspective effects, low-parallax geometry, very sparse matches, or deployment inside a full SfM/visual-odometry pipeline.

Presentation is generally clear but dense; the main result tables are crowded, several important implementation details are pushed to the supplement, and there are minor typos/inconsistencies such as '+C' versus '+F' in the ablation discussion. These are not central technical flaws but affect readability.

strengths: The paper tackles a difficult and practically relevant calibrated three-view relative-pose setting and offers simple solvers that can be implemented from standard 4-point affine, 5-point, and P3P components rather than relying on fragile large polynomial systems or learned homotopy continuation.

The mean-point construction is a clever pragmatic approximation: it is easy to implement, has some geometric justification, and the supplementary material explains why it contributes an additional perspective-camera constraint and provides a bounded epipolar-error argument.

The experimental evaluation is unusually broad for this type of geometry paper: PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen Day-Night are tested with many triplets, multiple RANSAC frameworks, synthetic/noise/outlier studies, threshold sensitivity, runtime measurements, ablations for delta/ENM/refinement/filtering, and an alternative three-pair pose metric.

The results support the main practical claim: with refinement and/or early non-minimal refitting, the proposed 4p3v variants generally outperform the HC 4p3v baseline and are competitive with or better than 5pt+P3P in RANSAC speed-accuracy trade-offs.

Reproducibility is stronger than average: the manuscript states that code and data are available, gives implementation details, specifies feature extraction/matching, RANSAC settings, thresholds, validation choices, and hardware for timing.
weaknesses: The contribution is primarily an approximate engineering solution, not a true minimal/exact solver for the 4p3v equations. The strongest performance often depends on local optimization, early non-minimal refitting, filtering, and extra heuristic hypotheses, so the standalone solver contribution is less clean than the title and framing may suggest.

The gains over a carefully enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline are sometimes modest. For example, the best M±delta variants improve AUC but can be substantially slower, and the 5pt+P3P+R+F+ENM baseline is often very close; this makes the practical advantage somewhat application-dependent.

The theoretical analysis of the mean-point approximation is useful but loose. Bounding the epipolar error by triangle size does not fully characterize when the approximation will be accurate, and the manuscript still relies heavily on empirical filtering and scene-dependent behavior.

The comparison to the older Nister-Schaffalitzky 4p3v method is incomplete because the authors could not run the epipole-curve sampling portion; the oracle discussion is informative but not a full empirical baseline.

Some evaluations are tied to a specific feature/matcher pipeline, calibrated COLMAP-derived poses, and sampled image triplets. A downstream SfM/localization experiment or evaluation across different matchers/inlier regimes would make the usefulness claim stronger.

The paper is dense and some tables/figures are hard to read in the provided PDF. There are also small presentation issues such as typos and duplicated table content, and the provided version is not anonymized, which would be a compliance issue for a double-blind submission.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely difficult and useful calibrated three-view relative pose setting, and the proposed decomposition into approximate two-view geometry plus P3P is simple, practical, and much easier to implement than prior homotopy-continuation or epipole-sampling approaches.

The mean-point correspondence idea is original and well motivated. The manuscript gives geometric intuition, a proof of a bounded epipolar-line error property, and ablations for the delta-shift, refinement, filtering, and early non-minimal refitting choices.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for this problem: three real datasets, many scenes and triplets, PoseLib and GC-RANSAC integrations, speed-accuracy curves, threshold sensitivity, outlier/noise experiments, and comparisons to both 4p3v(HC) and the strong 5pt+P3P baseline.

The best proposed variants consistently improve pose accuracy over the reported baselines. For example, in PoseLib, 4p3v(M+-delta)+R+F+ENM improves AUC@10 over 4p3v(HC) and 5pt+P3P across PhotoTourism, Cambridge, and Aachen. Code and data availability also support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The solvers are approximate rather than exact solutions to 4p3v, and the theoretical support does not guarantee pose accuracy. The mean-point bound is useful intuition but is loose and only concerns the epipolar error of the constructed correspondence, not the final three-camera pose.

The practical gains rely heavily on RANSAC-specific engineering: local optimization, refinement with the fourth third-view point, filtering, ENM, and the delta variants. The basic affine solver fails badly without ENM, and the basic mean-point solver is often close to or worse than 5pt+P3P.

The best-accuracy variants are not universally faster. In the early-termination PoseLib table, 4p3v(M+-delta)+R+F+ENM is substantially slower than 5pt+P3P on the aggregate datasets, so the advantage is best understood as a speed-accuracy tradeoff and a four-triplet sampling benefit rather than an outright faster replacement.

The comparison to the older Nister-Schaffalitzky epipole-curve method remains incomplete because the authors could not run the full code, and the evaluation uses one feature/matcher setup. This does not invalidate the results, but it leaves some uncertainty about generality across correspondence regimes and older baselines.

strengths: Addresses an important and difficult calibrated three-view relative pose setting, and the proposed 4p3v(A), 4p3v(M), and 4p3v(M±δ) solvers are practically appealing because they reduce the problem to well-known 4-point affine, 5-point essential matrix, and P3P components.

The mean-point pseudo-correspondence idea is simple, original enough in this context, and supported by a useful geometric argument plus synthetic and real-data evidence showing it is much better behaved than the affine approximation alone.

The evaluation is unusually broad for this geometry problem: PoseLib and GC-RANSAC, three real datasets, 18 scenes, 90k triplets, threshold sensitivity, outlier experiments, runtime measurements, and multiple ablations of δ, refinement, filtering, and early non-minimal refitting.

The paper compares against both the recent homotopy-continuation 4p3v solver and a strong 5pt+P3P baseline, including strengthened baseline variants with refinement/filtering/ENM, which makes the empirical claims more credible.
Reproducibility is strong: the manuscript gives implementation details, hyperparameter choices, hardware, code links, and data links.
weaknesses: The main solvers are approximate rather than exact 4p3v solvers. The initial 4p3v(A/M) stages effectively solve a relaxed or partial problem and rely on RANSAC, filtering, and local optimization to recover accuracy, so the theoretical contribution is less satisfying than a true stable minimal solver.

The theoretical analysis only weakly supports the accuracy claims. The bound for the mean-point correspondence is loose and depends on triangle geometry; it does not translate into a pose-error or convergence guarantee, and the paper itself acknowledges strong scene dependence before ENM/refinement.

The empirical gains over a carefully enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline are real but modest. For example, in the main PoseLib table the best proposed 4p3v(M±δ)+R+F+ENM improves AUC@10 only from 76.20 to 77.14 on PhotoTourism and from 66.31 to 66.95 on Cambridge, while often costing substantially more runtime than plain 5pt+P3P.

The strongest variants depend on a stack of engineering choices: δ sampling, filtering thresholds, LM refinement, ENM refitting, and RANSAC framework behavior. This somewhat blurs how much of the improvement comes from the core solver versus downstream optimization.

The comparison to the Nister-Schaffalitzky 4p3v method remains incomplete because the authors could not run the full epipole-sampling implementation and only discuss an oracle variant. This is understandable but leaves one historical baseline only partially evaluated.

Evaluation is concentrated on landmark/SfM-style image triplets with SuperPoint/LightGlue matches. The paper would be stronger with downstream SfM/localization impact, broader feature/matching regimes, or more analysis of degenerate cases such as planar scenes, tiny baselines, or very wide baselines.

Presentation is generally clear but very dense. The many solver variants and large tables make the main empirical message harder to parse, and some important caveats are pushed into supplementary material.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and difficult geometric estimation problem: relative pose of three calibrated cameras from four triplet correspondences. The motivation for practical approximate solvers is strong because exact/near-exact 4p3v approaches are complex, unstable, or hard to deploy in RANSAC-style pipelines.

The mean-point correspondence idea is easy to implement and is backed by a geometric explanation plus a proof that the induced epipolar line passes through the corresponding triangle.

The experimental evaluation is broad. The paper reports synthetic studies, noise and outlier experiments, ablations for the delta shift, refinement, filtering, ENM, threshold sensitivity, individual scene results, an alternative three-pair pose metric, and results in both PoseLib RANSAC and GC-RANSAC.

The evidence generally supports the practical claim: with refinement/filtering/ENM, the proposed 4p3v(M±delta)-based solvers often improve the speed-accuracy tradeoff over the HC 4p3v solver and over 5pt+P3P baselines on PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen Day-Night. Code and data links are provided, and the method is built from standard solvers, which helps reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core contribution is heuristic and approximate rather than a principled exact solution to 4p3v. The theoretical support for the mean-point approximation is limited: the epipolar-error bound is loose and does not characterize when the resulting pose estimate will be well conditioned, accurate, or fail.

The strongest results rely heavily on RANSAC local optimization, refinement on the fourth point, filtering, and early non-minimal refitting. Without these additions, some variants are weak: the pure affine 4p3v(A) solver has very large errors in PoseLib experiments, and the paper itself notes scene dependence for the approximate solvers.

The improvement over a carefully enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline is often modest once the same refinement/filtering/ENM ideas are added to that baseline. For example, in the main PoseLib table the best proposed variant improves AUC@10 only slightly over 5pt+P3P+R+F+ENM on several datasets, while sometimes costing substantially more runtime.

The technical development is reasonably supported: the paper explains why the mean-point constraint is not redundant for perspective cameras, gives a geometric bound on its epipolar error, and introduces sensible RANSAC-side refinements such as ENM, filtering, and short LM refinement.

The empirical evaluation is broad and convincing for a geometry paper: PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen; PoseLib and GC-RANSAC; synthetic noise, outlier, threshold sensitivity, runtime, and ablation studies. The best proposed variants generally improve accuracy and speed-accuracy tradeoffs over the HC solver and the basic 5pt+P3P baseline.

weaknesses: The central solver is approximate rather than an exact 4p3v solution. The provided error bound for the mean-point correspondence is quite loose and does not directly predict pose accuracy, degeneracies, or failure probability; the method still has non-zero error on noiseless instances.

The strongest gains over a strengthened 5pt+P3P baseline with the same refinement/filtering machinery are often modest, while the best M±δ variants can be noticeably slower in the early-termination tables. This somewhat tempers the practical impact claim.

Performance depends heavily on RANSAC integration, ENM, and local optimization. The standalone affine variant is weak, and even the mean-point solver is mainly compelling after the proposed refinement pipeline, so the contribution is as much a robust-estimation recipe as a solver.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and difficult geometric estimation problem: calibrated three-view relative pose from four triplet correspondences. The proposed strategy is practically appealing because it avoids brittle high-degree exact solvers and builds on well-tested 5-point, affine-F, and P3P components.

The mean-point approximate correspondence idea is simple, original enough for the problem setting, and well motivated geometrically. The supplement gives a useful bound on the epipolar error and explains why the mean-point constraint is non-redundant for perspective cameras.

The empirical evaluation is broad for this area: PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, Aachen Day-Night, synthetic/noise experiments, two RANSAC frameworks, threshold and outlier ablations, alternative pose metric, and per-scene speed-accuracy plots.

The strongest variant gives consistent gains over the reported 4p3v(HC) solver and over 5pt+P3P in the main PoseLib results, e.g. PhotoTourism AUC@10 improves from 74.30 for 5pt+P3P and 73.53 for HC to 77.14 for 4p3v(M±δ)+R+F+ENM. Code and data links are provided, which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core solver is approximate rather than an exact solution to 4p3v, and the theoretical support is limited. The epipolar-error bound for the mean point can be loose and does not characterize when the resulting pose estimate will be accurate or when RANSAC/LO will recover from a poor approximation.

Much of the performance depends on engineering around the approximate solver: ENM, filtering, LM refinement, local optimization, and the δ expansion. The unmodified affine solver is very weak, and the unmodified mean-point solver is often only comparable to or worse than 5pt+P3P, so the standalone algorithmic contribution is less decisive than the full pipeline results.

The best-performing 4p3v(M±δ)+R+F+ENM variant is substantially slower than the 5pt+P3P baseline in the PoseLib table, e.g. 112.60 ms vs 33.77 ms on PhotoTourism and 139.19 ms vs 53.34 ms on Aachen. The speed-accuracy tradeoff is favorable in plots, but the headline accuracy gains are sometimes modest relative to this added cost.

Comparison to prior solver [37] is incomplete because the authors could not run its full sampling procedure and only report an oracle-style discussion in the supplement. This is understandable, but it weakens claims about comprehensively surpassing prior 4p3v approaches.

The evaluation is strong on landmark-style calibrated image triplets, but less informative about degenerate or near-degenerate geometries, very planar scenes, extreme baselines, low texture, different feature matchers, or downstream SfM/localization impact. These limitations matter because the method's approximation quality is explicitly scene dependent.

Evaluation is unusually broad for this solver literature: PoseLib and GC-RANSAC, PhotoTourism/Cambridge/Aachen, synthetic stress tests, threshold sensitivity, outlier-ratio experiments, alternative pose-error metric, per-scene plots, and ablations of delta sampling, refinement, filtering, and early non-minimal refitting.

Reproducibility is strong: the manuscript states that code and data are available, and the algorithm is built from existing standard solvers rather than a fragile bespoke polynomial pipeline.
weaknesses: The central solvers are approximate rather than exact 4p3v solutions. Their correctness is supported mainly by geometric intuition and empirical behavior; there is no guarantee that the returned pose is close to the true solution outside favorable sampled configurations.

The empirical gains over the strongest 5pt+P3P baselines are consistent but relatively small: for example, the best PoseLib AUC@10 improvements over 5pt+P3P+R+F+ENM are about 0.9 on PhotoTourism, 0.6 on Cambridge, and 0.3 on Aachen, while runtime is often roughly 1.5-2x higher.

A substantial part of the final performance comes from RANSAC-level machinery, refinement, filtering, and ENM. This makes the solver contribution practically valuable but somewhat entangled with the robust-estimation wrapper, and the pure 4p3v(A) variant performs very poorly without ENM.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and genuinely difficult calibrated three-view relative pose setting. The proposed decomposition into approximate two-view geometry plus P3P is simple, practical, and well motivated for RANSAC-style use.

The mean-point correspondence idea is elegant: it converts the 4p3v setting into use of robust existing 5pt and P3P solvers, and the paper provides a useful geometric argument plus empirical validation that the approximation is often informative.

The evaluation is unusually broad for a minimal-solver paper: PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen Day-Night, many sampled triplets, two RANSAC frameworks, synthetic/noise/outlier studies, threshold sensitivity, ablations for delta, refinement, filtering, and early non-minimal refitting.

The authors compare against a strong 5pt+P3P baseline as well as the recent homotopy-continuation 4p3v solver, and they report both accuracy and runtime. Code and data availability substantially improve reproducibility.

The practical message is convincing: even if the pure approximate solvers are imperfect, the proposed variants with refinement/local optimization often outperform prior 4p3v alternatives and can give a favorable speed-accuracy tradeoff.
weaknesses: The core solvers are approximate rather than exact solutions to 4p3v. The theoretical analysis bounds the epipolar error of the mean-point correspondence in a limited geometric sense, but does not characterize pose error, failure modes, or when the approximation will be reliable.

The empirical gains over the strong 5pt+P3P baseline are often modest, especially after adding the same refinement/filtering/ENM machinery to the baseline. The best M±delta variants can be noticeably slower, so the advantage is mostly a pipeline-level speed-accuracy tradeoff rather than a uniformly better solver.

The contribution’s originality is somewhat incremental: much of the method is a clever recombination of existing 4pt affine, 5pt, P3P, RANSAC, ENM, and LM components. The novelty lies in the mean-point approximation and integration strategy, which is useful but not a major conceptual advance.

The comparison to Nister and Schaffalitzky [37] remains incomplete because the authors could not run the original sampling component and instead discuss an oracle/partial version. This is understandable but weakens claims about the full prior-art landscape.

Several claims depend heavily on local optimization, threshold choices, and inlier selection inside RANSAC. The paper acknowledges scene dependence, but the analysis of degeneracies, wide-baseline extremes, small triangles, near-planar/low-parallax cases, calibration error, and poor feature distributions remains limited.

Presentation is generally clear, but the main paper is dense and some tables/plots are hard to read; key conclusions sometimes require cross-referencing many appendix ablations. This is a presentation issue rather than a fatal technical flaw.

strengths: The paper targets a real and technically difficult calibrated three-view relative pose setting, and the idea of reducing 4p3v to existing 5-point/P3P or affine solvers is practically attractive.
The proposed solvers are simple to implement compared with homotopy-continuation or epipole-sampling approaches, and the manuscript provides code/data links.

The empirical section is broader than many geometry papers: PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, Aachen Day-Night, PoseLib, GC-RANSAC, ablations, threshold sensitivity, outlier experiments, and an alternative pose metric are reported.

Some refined variants improve over the reported HC solver and 5pt+P3P baseline, e.g. PoseLib AUC@10 improves from 74.30 to 77.14 on PhotoTourism and from 56.73 to 57.42 on Aachen for the strongest M±delta variant.
weaknesses: The core contribution is heuristic rather than a solution to the stated 4p3v problem. The mean-point correspondence is an affine/paraperspective approximation, and the provided bound only says the induced epipolar line intersects a triangle; it does not meaningfully bound pose error or characterize when the solver will succeed.

The raw proposed solvers are weak. In Table 2, 4p3v(A) catastrophically underperforms, and 4p3v(M) alone is below 5pt+P3P on all three datasets. Most gains come only after RANSAC-specific refinement, filtering, ENM, and local optimization, making it hard to attribute the improvement to the proposed minimal sample itself.

The comparison to 5pt+P3P is not fully convincing. The paper discards pairwise-only matches and evaluates on three-way correspondences, while 5pt+P3P can in principle exploit five matches in two views with only three visible in the third. This setup may overstate the practical advantage of sampling four triplets.

The accuracy improvements over a strengthened 5pt+P3P baseline are modest, while the best M±delta+R+F+ENM variant is much slower in early-termination PoseLib results, e.g. 112.60 ms vs 33.77 ms on PhotoTourism and 139.19 ms vs 53.34 ms on Aachen.

The paper repeatedly claims state-of-the-art performance, but the evidence is sensitive to solver variants and runtime regime. Some variants trade accuracy for speed, some need ENM, and the affine solver only becomes competitive after substantial refitting.

Important failure modes are not sufficiently analyzed: planar or near-planar points, very small baselines, pure/near-pure rotation, degenerate triangles for the mean point, wide-baseline perspective effects, and scenes where the synthetic correspondence is systematically biased.

The comparison to Nister and Schaffalitzky [37] remains weak because the practical solver could not be run; the oracle discussion is informative but not an empirical baseline. This leaves an important historical comparator unresolved.

The presentation is dense and sometimes overclaims relative to the evidence; the main tables are hard to read, and the distinction between a solver contribution and a RANSAC pipeline contribution is not made cleanly enough.
